title: A different kind of skyline.
text: The Statue of Unity rises above the Narmada landscape in Kevadia. At 182 metres, the monument to Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel is the world's tallest statue.

title: Small islands. A lot of sea.
text: India's smallest union territory has just 32 square kilometres of land across an archipelago of 36 islands. Its name means a hundred thousand islands.

title: Bridges that keep growing.
text: Khasi communities guide living tree roots across streams to grow bridges. The craft is passed between generations, and the structures can strengthen as they mature.

title: A city, not just a monument.
text: Hampi was a capital of the Vijayanagara Empire. More than 1,600 surviving remains include temples, markets, waterworks, and royal buildings.

title: A national park that floats.
text: Keibul Lamjao, on the southern part of Loktak Lake, is the world's only floating national park. It is also the last natural habitat of the sangai.

title: Seven monuments, one former capital.
text: Old Goa's World Heritage property brings together seven churches and convents. Among them is the Basilica of Bom Jesus, which houses the tomb of Francis Xavier.

title: A village that gave dance its name.
text: Kuchipudi takes its name from the Andhra Pradesh village where it originated. One of India's classical dance forms, it brings dance and drama together in a single performance tradition.

title: Eight centuries of asking questions.
text: Nalanda sustained organized learning for roughly 800 years. Its surviving monasteries, shrines, and teaching spaces reveal an institution whose educational model influenced others across Asia.

title: The harvest below sea level.
text: In Kuttanad, rice grows in reclaimed fields below sea level. This farming system, shaped around the backwaters, received recognition as a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System in 2013.

title: A gallery before galleries.
text: Bhimbetka's sandstone shelters hold paintings spanning the Mesolithic era through later historical periods. Five clusters of shelters preserve traces of how people lived with this landscape over millennia.

title: Bamboo sets the rhythm.
text: Cheraw, a traditional Mizo dance, is performed with pairs of bamboo poles held across supports on the ground. The bamboo is part of the performance itself, not simply a backdrop.

title: Ten days, many traditions.
text: Held from 1 to 10 December, the Hornbill Festival brings together the traditions of Nagaland's ethnic groups. That gathering is why it is often called the Festival of Festivals.

title: A roof with a lighter touch.
text: The 13th-century Ramappa Temple at Palampet uses lightweight, porous bricks in its tower to reduce the load above. Below them, finely carved figures record dance traditions of the Kakatiya period.

title: Two very different Himalayas.
text: The Valley of Flowers and Nanda Devi National Parks share one World Heritage listing. Alpine flower meadows in one contrast with the steep, remote mountain wilderness of the other.

title: A monastery on a mountain scale.
text: Tawang is home to India's largest Buddhist monastery. Set above the Tawang Chu valley, it is a reminder of the region's deep connections with Himalayan Buddhist traditions.

title: A landscape the river keeps rewriting.
text: At Kaziranga, the Brahmaputra's floods reshape banks, pools, and grasslands. These changing habitats support the world's largest population of Indian one-horned rhinoceroses, a major conservation recovery from the early 20th century.

title: The same waterfall, a different season.
text: The Indravati drops about 90 feet over Chitrakote's horseshoe-shaped ledge. Its appearance changes with the seasons: rainy-day water can look reddish, while the summer cascade looks pale under moonlight.

title: Long before the modern city.
text: An archaeological site and a living village share the name Rakhigarhi. Its remains span pre-Harappan, early Harappan, and mature Harappan phases, revealing several chapters of the Indus Valley Civilisation.

title: History, with a window seat.
text: The Kalka-Shimla Railway winds through the Himalayan foothills for about 96 kilometres. This working mountain railway shares a World Heritage listing with the Darjeeling Himalayan and Nilgiri Mountain railways.

title: A place name becomes a dance style.
text: Seraikella in Jharkhand lends its name to one of Chhau's three regional styles. The dance blends martial and folk traditions, with related forms taking their names from Purulia and Mayurbhanj.

title: A lake with an arrival from space.
text: Lonar Lake fills a crater made by a meteorite impact in present-day Buldhana district. Its saline, alkaline waters now form a protected wetland recognized as a Ramsar site.

title: Twenty-four wheels, carved in stone.
text: Konark's 13th-century Sun Temple was conceived as Surya's chariot. Its twelve pairs of carved wheels turn the building into a monumental image of the sun god's journey across the sky.

title: Heritage in the kitchen cupboard.
text: In Jandiala Guru, the Thathera community makes traditional brass and copper utensils. UNESCO recognized this craft in 2014, placing the skills behind everyday objects on its Intangible Cultural Heritage list.

title: Architecture for reading the sky.
text: Jaipur's Jantar Mantar is a collection of enormous astronomical instruments built in the early 18th century. Its masonry structures were designed to measure celestial positions through naked-eye observation.

title: A mountain with more than one meaning.
text: Khangchendzonga National Park is recognized for both natural and cultural heritage. Its peaks, lakes, and forests also hold sacred meanings in Lepcha and Buddhist traditions, inseparable from the landscape itself.

title: An extra rail for the climb.
text: The Nilgiri Mountain Railway uses rack-and-pinion traction to negotiate steep gradients. Completed in 1908, its roughly 46-kilometre route climbs from 326 to 2,203 metres above sea level.

title: The hillside is the canvas.
text: At Unakoti, images of Hindu deities are carved into the rock itself. The bas-relief sculptures at this Shaivite site are dated on stylistic grounds to the 7th-9th centuries, before the Manikya dynasty.

title: The first rain, bottled.
text: Kannauj's perfume makers produce mitti attar using earth as an ingredient. Its scent recalls petrichor, the distinctive smell when rain first meets dry ground, alongside the city's better-known floral fragrances.

title: A classroom beneath the trees.
text: Rabindranath Tagore began his school at Santiniketan in 1901, with open-air classrooms under tree canopies. Nature, music, and art were central to the educational vision that later grew into Visva-Bharati.

title: Ancient iron, enduring science.
text: The iron pillar in Delhi's Qutb complex is about 1,600 years old. Its resistance to corrosion comes from a protective surface film and the properties of its iron, evidence of sophisticated early metalworking.

title: One territory, four separate places.
text: Puducherry is more than its namesake town. The territory includes Puducherry and Karaikal beside Tamil Nadu, Mahe on the Kerala coast, and Yanam adjoining Andhra Pradesh, scattered across both sides of southern India.

title: Beyond the beaches, a volcano.
text: Barren Island is an uninhabited volcanic island in the Andaman Sea. It contains India's only confirmed active volcano, a reminder that these islands have a geological story beyond their beaches.

title: A second life for broken things.
text: Nek Chand began Chandigarh's Rock Garden in his spare time, turning discarded household and industrial materials into sculpture. What started as a private project grew into a public landmark.

place: Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu
title: An alliance written in stone.
text: Diu Fort was built in 1535 after an alliance between Gujarat's Sultan Bahadur Shah and the Portuguese. On the island's eastern tip, it records a chapter of the region's maritime history.

title: Vegetable patches that float.
text: Dal Lake's floating gardens are built from mats of vegetation and earth. Anchored on the water, these nutrient-rich plots support crops such as tomatoes and cucumbers, an unexpected side of Srinagar's famous lake.

title: A higher place to look up.
text: Hanle's Indian Astronomical Observatory sits about 4,500 metres above sea level. Operated by the Indian Institute of Astrophysics, it hosts telescopes that observe the universe in optical, infrared, and gamma-ray light.
